newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore port limits extension to curb OPL - MPA.
newsitem.headline: Singapore port limits extension to curb OPL - MPA.

text.p: Singapore extended its port limit in early July to curb refuelling of ships outside its port limits, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore (MPA) said.

"The Singapore port limits was extended to enable the MPA to better cope with the increasing number of vessel calls at the port and to reduce undesirable outside port limits activities," the MPA said in a written reply to a Reuters query.
"With this extension, more vessels can anchor within the port. We encourage vessels conducting bunkering to take advantage of this increased anchorage space for their bunkering operations."
The extension of the port limits is still within Singapore waters, MPA said.
Industry sources said the MPA had been trying for some time to discourage off-port-limits (OPL) bunkering which was unregulated and posed an environmental danger to Singapore.
They also said the quality and quantity of bunker fuel sold off-port-limits are not guaranteed.
But they said that despite the dangers, OPL bunker sales were rising strongly and eating into Singapore's regulated bunker business because the fuel was cheaper and did not have to pay port fees.

Official data showed Singapore's bunker sales totalled 16.9 million tonnes in 1996, a three-percent drop from 1995 against a doubling of the OPL market over the same period to three million tonnes, industry sources said.
They said the MPA extended port limits on the southern and eastern seaboards on July 11 and that shippers were informed on July 25.
The new boundaries extended the port limit southward by three miles off Singapore's southeastern and eastern coasts, a bunker trader said.
On the southwestern coast, the port limit was also extended southwards by one mile, the traders said.
The movement squeezes the open seas between the port limits and the traffic separation zone, the highway for shipping between Singapore and Indonesia.
Traders said OPL bunker demand had fallen since the port limits were extended and Indonesia moved around the same time to stamp out unauthorised refuelling in Indonesian waters.
In July, the Indonesian authorities boarded several tankers refuelling outside Singapore port limits.
